claim_scope: A documented Qianlong yangcai ceramic for comparing dense ornament organized by vessel zones, borders and hierarchy, within the museum-documented court craft context. Not proof of a particular emperor’s personal use, a universal court palette, or all Chinese ornament.

limits: One frontal vessel view, not the underside, internal mechanism or all decorated media. Rotation, assembly, reign and named motifs are museum documentation, not demonstrated operation. No individual court commission, personal imperial use, precise year, hidden craftsmanship or material authenticity is independently established. Dense flowers, dragons, gold color or a reign mark alone cannot identify an unrelated object as imperial.
observable_features: A single complete vessel is isolated against a plain gray background; no visitors, cases or labels obscure it.
Dark blue-and-gold neck and shoulder fields contrast with a lighter, densely patterned openwork belly.
Pink dragon-like forms and intertwined floral scrolls fill the central belly, bounded by distinct bands above and below.
The narrower lower body and foot repeat gold scroll and leaf-like bands, organizing abundant ornament into a neck–shoulder–belly–foot hierarchy.

association_evidence.supports: The National Palace Museum identifies this exact accession, title and Qianlong reign date; describes the four-part revolving construction, dragon/lotus ornament and three decorative zones; supplies the exact public image and open-data image policy. It does not document this piece’s personal use by a named emperor.

The museum’s description of the 2008 Qianlong yangcai exhibition catalog places its collected yangcai and painted-enamel porcelain types in Qing court craftsmanship. The exact object record cites this catalog. This supports the type’s court craft context, not an individually documented commission or user.

confusion_check.shared_appearances: Axes, dragons, flowers, gold and dense patterns occur outside historical court work.
confusion_check.discriminating_relationships: Compare documented historical context together with the visible hierarchy of bounded ornamental fields. Here ornament is abundant but zoned by the vessel’s neck, shoulder, belly and foot; it is not merely a dragon symbol applied to a generic object. Pair with the robe for another medium, without treating either as all court design.
confusion_check.cannot_conclude: The view cannot authenticate a new object, prove all-over patterns are imperial, or make a Qianlong mark on an unrelated piece genuine.
